newsitem.title: UK: Investors still warm to Bulgarian Bradys.
newsitem.headline: Investors still warm to Bulgarian Bradys.

text.p: The little enthusiasm there was in early Tuesday trading in the emerging debt market was mainly directed at Bulgaria which touched new highs.
Russian debt also strengthened and Latin paper was mostly a touch firmer.
Bulgarian IABs were traded at a record 63 cents in the dollar, up about 3/4 of a point from the New York close.
Since the decision to hold early elections -- seen as crucial if there was to be any hope of preventing economic and political chaos -- the price of Bulgarian debt has jumped about a third.
Even though few doubt there are serious problems ahead, the risk of default is seen to have declined sharply, traders said.
"It could still get ugly there. But you have to look at it against a backdrop of the rest of the market where spreads are incredibly tight. Everyone is chasing yield," a European bank trader said.
"How high the price can go is anyone's guess. But I know there are a few shorts out there who are in a bit of pain," he added.
Spreads on Bulgarian discount bonds have narrowed from 1,750 basis points over U.S. Treasuries to around 1,000 this year.
International Monetary Fund officials are back in Sofia to negotiate a deal on funding which has to be in place before Bulgaria can expect financing from other areas, including the European Union.
Russia continues firmer in the run-up to the closing of its agreement with London Club creditors.
Vneshekonombank dollar debt was up 3/8 of a point at 85-1/2 percent of face value.

Traders generally expect the price to rise further, albeit gradually, with one saying it could reach the high 80s. He said the price was still cheap when compared with spreads on major Latin American Bradys.
